Zechariah is speaking of powerful rulers as if they were a cedar tree that had fallen. A cedar was one of the tallest, strongest trees in that area, so a fallen cedar pictures a powerful ruler who has lost his power.

The word translated as fortified has a similar spelling to the word for vintage/grape harvest. Some ancient manuscripts and versions read this as “the forest of the vintage,” apparently confusing the two similar words.
11:3: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The word for glory here is a lot like the word for the “majestic ones” in verse 2. Zechariah repeats this idea to show that everything great and important, both the leaders and the land, has been completely ruined.
Zechariah is speaking of the rulers of the land as if they were shepherds and young lions that were wailing and roaring over what they had lost.
Zechariah is using the pride of the Jordan as a common expression of the culture to mean the dense thickets of trees and bushes that grow along the Jordan River.
11:4: The Lord is speaking of leading and caring for the people as if that task were to Shepherd a flock of sheep.
The Lord is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a flock of sheep.
11:5: אֲשֶׁר קֹנֵיהֶן יַהֲרְגֻן וְלֹא יֶאְשָׁמוּ וּמֹכְרֵיהֶן יֹאמַר
Here the Lord is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next.
11:6: אָנֹכִי מַמְצִיא אֶת־הָאָדָם אִישׁ בְּיַד־רֵעֵהוּ וּבְיַד מַלְכּוֹ
Here the Lord is speaking as if he were causing people to fall into the power of their neighbors and king, as though pushing them down so that others could seize them.
11:7: לְאַחַד קָרָאתִי נֹעַם וּלְאַחַד קָרָאתִי חֹבְלִים
The words Favor and Union are names that Zechariah gave to his two shepherd’s staffs. He chose names that carry meaning, since the staffs represent the Lord’s relationship with the people.
11:8: The implication is that these three shepherds were leaders of the people whom the Lord removed from their position.
Zechariah is using my soul became short with them as a common expression of the culture to mean that he became impatient with them.
11:9: Zechariah is speaking of the people as if they were sheep that would eat the flesh of one another. He means mean that they will turn against and destroy one another.
11:10: Zechariah is using the word cut as a common expression of the culture to mean “make,” since in that culture people spoke of making a covenant as cutting it.
This could mean: (1) all the nations of the world. (2) the Israelite nation.
11:12: In ancient times, a piece of silver was a coin or weight of silver called a shekel, which weighed about 11 grams, or about a third of an ounce.
11:13: A potter is a kind of craftsman who forms objects out of clay.

The Lord actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here, since thirty pieces of silver was in fact a contemptibly small price. It was also the amount the owner of an ox that gored a slave to death had to give to the owner of the slave (see Exo 21:32), so by paying that amount they were saying he was worth the same as a dead slave.
11:15: The Lord is speaking of a ruler of the people as if he were a shepherd.
11:16: Zechariah uses a repetitive series of clauses here to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming.
Here Zechariah is speaking as if the strongest, healthiest members of the people were the fat one, a well-fed sheep.
The Lord is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
11:17: Here, his arm represents the shepherd’s strength and his right eye represents his ability to see.
זְרֹעוֹ יָבוֹשׁ תִּיבָשׁ וְעֵין יְמִינוֹ כָּהֹה תִכְהֶה
The Lord is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
12:1: Here Zechariah is speaking of the message from the Lord as if it were a burden, that is, a heavy load that a person must carry.
Here Zechariah is speaking of how the Lord made the world as if he were stretching out a tent to form the heavens and founding a building to form the earth.
This phrase continues the references to creation.
12:2: Zechariah is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
Here the Lord is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were a cup of staggering, that is, a cup of wine that would make the surrounding nations drunk so that they reel and cannot stand.
This could mean: (1) Judah and Jerusalem are besieged. (2) Judah is going to besiege Jerusalem.
12:3: Here the Lord is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were a stone of burden, that is, a stone so heavy that anyone who tries to lift it injures himself.
12:4: Here the Lord is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were a house, a single household.
כָל־סוּס בַּתִּמָּהוֹן וְרֹכְבוֹ בַּשִּׁגָּעוֹן … וְכֹל סוּס הָעַמִּים
The Lord is using every horse, every horse of the peoples, and its rider to represent the whole army of the enemy nations.
12:5: This could mean: (1) the people who live in Jerusalem are strong because the Lord of Armies their God is with them or (2) the people who live in Jerusalem are a source of strength for the chiefs of Judah.
12:6: כְּכִיּוֹר אֵשׁ בְּעֵצִים וּכְלַפִּיד אֵשׁ בְּעָמִיר

The point of this comparison is that just as a basin of fire among trees and a torch of fire in a sheaf quickly burn up everything around them, so the chiefs of Judah will destroy the peoples around them.
A basin is a kind of large, open container that can hold burning coals or fire.
A sheaf is a bundle of cut grain stalks tied together. When dried, it is highly flammable.
Here the Lord is speaking of the chiefs of Judah destroying their enemies as if they would devour them the way fire consumes what it burns.
The Lord is referring to every direction by naming two major components, the right and the left.
Here, Jerusalem represents the people who live in Jerusalem.
12:7: Here, the tents of Judah represents the homes and households of the people of Judah.
Here Zechariah is speaking of the descendants of King David, the royal family, as if they were a house, a single household.
12:8: Here Zechariah is speaking of a weak or feeble person as if he were a stumbler.
Zechariah says will be like David, and the house of David, like God as an extreme statement for emphasis.
The point of this comparison is that just as God and the angel of the Lord are powerful, so the house of David will be powerful as they lead the people.
Here, their face represents their presence, so the phrase means going ahead of the people to lead them.
12:10: Here the Lord is speaking of generously giving his spirit to people as if he would pour out a liquid on them.
The point of this comparison is that just as people grieve very deeply for the only one, that is, an only child who has died, so the people will mourn over the one whom they pierced.
The point of this comparison is that just as people grieve bitterly over the firstborn, that is, a firstborn son who has died, so the people will grieve bitterly over the one whom they pierced.
12:11: The point of this comparison is that just as the mourning of Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo was a well-known time of very great grief, so the mourning in Jerusalem will be very great.
This could mean: (1) the weeping for King Josiah, who was killed at Megiddo and for whom the people mourned greatly, or (2) the ritual mourning for a god named Hadad Rimmon, or (3) both.
The word Hadad Rimmon is the name of a place, and the word Megiddo is the name of a place.
12:12: Here, the land represents the people who live in the land.
This could mean: (1) Nathan, the son of King David, or (2) Nathan, the prophet who served during David’s reign.
12:13: The word Shimeite is the name of a people group, the descendants of a man named Shimei.
13:1: Here Zechariah is speaking as if the means of cleansing from sin were a fountain that would be opened.
Here, the house of David represents the descendants of David and the royal dynasty.
Zechariah is referring to all types of uncleanness by naming two major components, sin and impurity.
13:2: Here, the names of the idols represents the memory and reputation of the idols.
13:3: Here, the name of the Lord represents the authority of the Lord.
13:4: The implication is that a cloak of hair was the distinctive garment that prophets wore, so putting it on was a way of claiming to be a prophet.
13:5: This could mean: (1) that the person is tied to this land and working this land because he is a bondservant or slave to the owner. (2) that he owns this land (requires reading the Hebrew slightly differently). That is, he’s a small landowner or a subsistence farmer and is tied to the land.
13:6: This could mean: (1) that the speaker is saying he was injured somehow while at the home of friends, perhaps in a drunken brawl or something. (2) that the speaker is speaking of the false gods that he worshiped as if they were his lovers. Idol worship sometimes involves self-mutilation.
13:7: The Lord is speaking to a Sword that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that is coming on his shepherd.
Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man, my companion—the Lord is using the term Sword to represent the violent death that a sword can inflict.
The Lord is speaking of the leader of his people as if he were a shepherd.
The Lord is speaking of his people as if they were a flock of sheep.
Here, hand represents the power of the Lord.
13:8: The Lord is speaking of people being killed as if they were parts of something that could be cut off, such as cutting branches from a tree.
The Lord is speaking of the people who will die as if their lives were a breath that will expire, or run out.
13:9: The Lord is speaking of the suffering he will use to purify his people as if it were a fire.
וּצְרַפְתִּים כִּצְרֹף אֶת־הַכֶּסֶף וּבְחַנְתִּים כִּבְחֹן אֶת־הַזָּהָב

The point of this comparison is that just as one refines the silver and tests the gold to remove impurities and prove them genuine, so the Lord will purify his people through suffering and prove that they are genuine.

The implication is that He is my people and The Lord is my God are the words of a covenant, expressing the restored relationship in which the Lord claims these people as his own and they acknowledge him as their God.
14:1: Zechariah is using the term Behold to focus the attention of his listeners on what he is about to say.

Zechariah is speaking to the city of Jerusalem, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about what will happen to the city.
14:2: The oral reading tradition of the original language substitutes a less explicit word here, referring in a polite way to what the soldiers will do to the women.
Zechariah is speaking as if the rest of the people would literally not be cut off from the city. He means that the enemies will not remove them from it.
14:3: The point of this comparison is that just as the Lord fought powerfully for his people on a day of battle in the past, so he will fight against these nations.
14:4: Zechariah is using his feet, one part of the Lord, to represent all of the Lord.
14:5: The implication is that this was a well-known earthquake that the people of Judah still remembered.
14:6: The implication is that the normal sources of light will fail on that day. This could mean: (1) that there will be no light and that instead there will be cold and frost, or (2) that the bright heavenly bodies will no longer shine.
14:7: Zechariah is using the two parts of a full day, day and night, to mean the entire cycle of time.
14:8: Zechariah is using the two main seasons of the year, the summer and the winter, to mean the whole year.
14:9: The implication is that people everywhere will worship the Lord alone and honor him alone as God.
Here, his name represents the Lord himself and his reputation.
14:10: Zechariah is using the two extremes of the land of Judah, Geba in the north and Rimmon in the south, to mean all of the land between them.
The point of this comparison is that just as the Arabah is a flat plain, so the land around Jerusalem will become flat.
The words the Gate of Benjamin, the First Gate, the Gate of the Corners, and the Tower of Hananel are the names of places in Jerusalem.
Zechariah is referring to all of Jerusalem by naming two extremes, the Gate of Benjamin and the winepresses of the king.
14:11: The implication is that enemies will never again devote Jerusalem to complete destruction in war.
Jerusalem is spoken of as a living thing. By referring to the city in this way, the meaning is that its name represents the people who live in Jerusalem.
14:13: Zechariah is using each man will seize the hand of his neighbor as a common expression of the culture to mean that people will panic and attack one another in confusion.
14:14: The implication is that the people of Judah will take part in this battle. This could mean: (1) that they will fight at Jerusalem alongside its people against the nations; or (2) that they will fight against Jerusalem along with the nations.
14:16: Bowing down before someone was a symbolic action by which a person showed honor and submission to a ruler.
The Festival of Booths is a kind of yearly celebration during which the Israelites lived in temporary shelters for a week to remember how their ancestors lived after they came out of Egypt.
14:17: The implication is that without rain the crops of those people will fail, and so this will be a punishment for them.
14:18: The terms does not go up and does not come mean similar things. Zechariah is using the two terms together for emphasis.

This could mean: (1) the Lord will judge Egypt by plague instead of withholding rain, since rain is not how Egypt grows crops. (2) the Lord will also withhold rain from southern Egypt that feeds the Nile River that the people of Egypt water their crops from rather than from direct rain.
14:19: זֹאת תִּהְיֶה חַטַּאת מִצְרָיִם וְחַטַּאת כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם
Here, the sin represents the punishment for sin.
14:20: The implication is that things which were very common will become holy. Someone will engrave the words “Holy to the Lord” on the bells, just as those words were engraved on the turban of the high priest. To transfer something so holy to something so common would have been somewhat shocking to the original audience.
וְהָיָה הַסִּירוֹת בְּבֵית יְהוָה כַּמִּזְרָקִים לִפְנֵי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
The point of this comparison is that just as the bowls that the priests use at the altar are sacred, so the pots in the house of the Lord will be sacred.
14:21: Here, a Canaanite represents someone who does not belong in the house of the Lord. This could mean: (1) a trader or merchant, since the Canaanites were well known as traders, or (2) an unclean foreigner.
